title: Biological Effects of Radiation
lead: Ionizing radiation carries enough energy to break bonds and knock electrons out of the molecules of living cells. This section separates it from nonionizing radiation, compares how far each kind of radiation penetrates matter, and names the instruments and the units used to measure activity, absorbed dose and tissue damage.
objectives: Describe the biological impact of ionizing radiation
Define units for measuring radiation exposure
Explain the operation of common tools for detecting radioactivity
List common sources of radiation exposure in the US
summary_html:
We are constantly exposed to radiation from a variety of naturally occurring and human-produced sources. This radiation can affect living organisms. Ionizing radiation is the most harmful because it can ionize molecules or break chemical bonds, which damages the molecule and causes malfunctions in cell processes. It can also create reactive hydroxyl radicals that damage biological molecules and disrupt physiological processes. Radiation can cause somatic or genetic damage, and is most harmful to rapidly reproducing cells. Types of radiation differ in their ability to penetrate material and damage tissue, with alpha particles the least penetrating but potentially most damaging and gamma rays the most penetrating.

Various devices, including Geiger counters, scintillators, and dosimeters, are used to detect and measure radiation, and monitor radiation exposure. We use several units to measure radiation: becquerels or curies for rates of radioactive decay; gray or rads for energy absorbed; and rems or sieverts for biological effects of radiation. Exposure to radiation can cause a wide range of health effects, from minor to severe, and including death. We can minimize the effects of radiation by shielding with dense materials such as lead, moving away from the source, and limiting time of exposure.

Ionizing radiation can (a) directly damage a biomolecule by ionizing it or breaking its bonds, or (b) create an H<sub>2</sub>O<sup>+</sup> ion, which reacts with H<sub>2</sub>O to form a hydroxyl radical, which in turn reacts with the biomolecule, causing damage indirectly.

exercises.prompt: Tritium is a radioactive isotope of hydrogen (t1/2 = 12.32 y) that has several uses, including self-powered lighting, in which electrons emitted in tritium radioactive decay cause phosphorus to glow. Its nucleus contains one proton and two neutrons, and the atomic mass of tritium is 3.016 amu. What is the activity of a sample containing 1.00mg of tritium (a) in Bq and (b) in Ci?

If a hospital were storing radioisotopes, what is the minimum containment needed to protect against:
(a) cobalt-60 (a strong γ emitter used for irradiation)
(b) molybdenum-99 (a beta emitter used to produce technetium-99 for imaging)

answer.solution: (a) Cobalt-60 needs thick shielding of a dense, high atomic number element such as lead, or a very thick layer of concrete. γ rays are the most penetrating radiation in Figure 21.33: they pass through a thick layer of most materials, and some pass through a few feet of concrete, but lead attenuates them effectively with a thinner barrier. The isotope must be kept in a lead container or a room walled with lead. (b) Molybdenum-99 needs only a thin layer of metal. β particles pass through a hand or a thin layer of paper or wood but are stopped by a thin layer of metal, so a closed metal container, such as one of aluminum a few millimeters thick, stops its radiation.

exercises.prompt: Based on what is known about Radon-222’s primary decay method, why is inhalation so dangerous?

answer.solution: Alpha particles can be stopped by very thin shielding but have much stronger ionizing potential than beta particles, X-rays, and γ-rays. When inhaled, there is no protective skin covering the cells of the lungs, making it possible to damage the DNA in those cells and cause cancer.

exercises.prompt: Given specimens uranium-232 (t1/2 = 68.9 y) and uranium-233 (t1/2 = 159,200 y) of equal mass, which one would have greater activity and why?

answer.solution: Uranium-232 has the greater activity, about 2.32 × 10<sup>3</sup> times that of uranium-233. The activity is $\klamdecay N$, with $\klamdecay=\text{ln 2}/\kthalf$. Equal masses of the two isotopes hold nearly the same number of nuclei, since their molar masses are nearly the same; the ratio of nuclei, uranium-232 to uranium-233, is 233/232 = 1.004. The decay constants are in the inverse ratio of the half-lives, (159,200 y)/(68.9 y) = 2.311 × 10<sup>3</sup>, so a uranium-232 nucleus is about 2300 times as likely to decay in a given second. The ratio of activities is the product, 1.004 × 2.311 × 10<sup>3</sup> = 2.32 × 10<sup>3</sup>. The much shorter half-life makes uranium-232 the more active sample.

exercises.prompt:
A scientist is studying a 2.234 g sample of thorium-229 (t1/2 = 7340 y) in a laboratory.
(a) What is its activity in Bq?
(b) What is its activity in Ci?
Given specimens neon-24 (t1/2 = 3.38 min) and bismuth-211 (t1/2 = 2.14 min) of equal mass, which one would have greater activity and why?

answer.solution: Neon-24 has the greater activity, about 5.6 times that of bismuth-211. The activity is $\klamdecay N$, with $\klamdecay=\text{ln 2}/\kthalf$, so both the number of nuclei and the decay constant must be compared. Equal masses hold numbers of nuclei in the inverse ratio of the molar masses, about 24 g/mol and 211 g/mol, so the neon sample holds 211/24 = 8.79 times as many nuclei. Bismuth-211 has the shorter half-life, so its decay constant is larger, by 3.38 min/2.14 min = 1.58. The ratio of activities, neon-24 to bismuth-211, is 8.79/1.58 = 5.57. The far greater number of neon nuclei outweighs the somewhat faster decay of bismuth.

footnotes.html: The book writes 1 Ci = 3.7 × 10<sup>11</sup> decay/s, here and in the line below. The curie is 3.7 × 10<sup>10</sup> decay/s, as the section defines it, and the activity is $2.10 \times 10^{14}$ Bq ÷ $3.7 \times 10^{10}$ Bq/Ci = 5.7 × 10<sup>3</sup> Ci.
